channel_name: No Priors · Elad Gil & Sarah Guo
video_title: Taking on ServiceNow: Coding Agents for the Rest of Us with Serval Co-Founder and CEO Jake Stauch
gist: Serval co-founder/CEO Jake Stauch explains how his 2.5-year-old, 200-person company is attacking ServiceNow head-on with a code-generation platform that lets IT teams build enterprise automations, positioning Serval as the governance 'boundary' (approvals, just-in-time access, audit trail, SDLC) that lets large enterprises adopt agents safely. He predicts tighter least-privilege permissions as agents proliferate, a SaaS consolidation that kills point solutions but not core systems of record, and continued rising AI spend despite a post-'token maxing' pullback.

insights.claim: Serval set out from day one to beat ServiceNow head-on and become the largest enterprise software company of all time, rather than building an AI layer on top of incumbents or going down-market.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: A direct system-of-record replacement strategy targets the largest prize but requires enterprise-grade product from the start.
insights.quote: We circled Service Now and we said we're going to beat them and we're going to build something much bigger.

insights.claim: IT teams frequently cite ServiceNow as both what they spend the most on and what they hate most, because it is hard to build on, needs consultants, runs 6-12 months behind needs, and keeps getting more expensive.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Customer frustration plus rising cost creates an opening for AI-native ITSM challengers.
insights.quote: it's always kind of running 6 to 12 months behind where you want it to be

insights.claim: Stauch argues building an AI layer on top of incumbents caps a startup's upside (with Veeva's backward integration off Salesforce cited as a rare exception), while going down-market like Rippling or HubSpot takes about a decade.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval) / host
insights.so_what: Layer-on-top AI startups face structural ceilings versus incumbents.

insights.claim: Serval's founding bet was that code is the right way to express enterprise automation, better than drag-and-drop builders, and that coding agents would get good at deterministic procedural scripts because they are a verifiable domain that hill-climbs well.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: AI code generation erodes the moat of workflow-builder platforms like ServiceNow.
insights.quote: code was the right way to express automation in the enterprise

insights.claim: Early on Serval had to seed LLMs with libraries of example workflows, but models improved until it became hard to give them a workflow they could not automate if the APIs existed.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Capability gains in coding models directly expanded the automation market.

insights.claim: Fox Corporation adopted Serval company-wide, and the employee who led the migration was nominated MVP of the entire company, which Stauch uses to pitch Serval as a career-making move.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Large enterprise wins signal ServiceNow displacement is real at scale.

insights.claim: Serval is about two and a half years old, has 200 employees, and expects hiring velocity to increase because more productive employees justify hiring more, not fewer.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: AI productivity gains may increase rather than reduce headcount at fast-growing AI companies.
insights.quote: because every employee is so much more productive, we actually want more of them, not less of them

insights.claim: Stauch says Serval does not build LLMs but the guardrails, and smarter models make enterprises want to clamp down harder on boundaries, making Serval more valuable as intelligence improves.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Governance layers are a beneficiary rather than a victim of model progress.
insights.quote: Serval is the boundary. Serval is the guardrails.

insights.claim: Stauch predicts enterprises will shrink employee permissions to true least privilege because agents amplify the damage any over-permissioned user can do, and the layer that grants exceptions with approvals and audit trails becomes essential.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Privilege-escalation and identity governance become key control points in agentic enterprise.
insights.quote: I actually think access is going to get more and more controlled for individuals in the enterprise.

insights.claim: Personal workforce agents such as OpenAI's offerings work well for consumers, SMB and mid-market, but in large enterprises individual permissions are so limited that personal agents are not very useful.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Consumer-style agents face a hard ceiling in large enterprise without an admin-level governance layer.

insights.claim: Most new AI products ship agents straight to production, but large regulated enterprises require a full SDLC with dev, staging, prod, review and user acceptance testing, which Serval builds in.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Enterprise-grade release processes are a differentiator many AI startups never build.

insights.claim: Background agents are the 'ultimate moonshot in enterprise software' but no one has made them safe; letting them write arbitrary code against systems is an unbounded security risk, so Serval uses incremental approval of deterministic tools.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Fully autonomous enterprise agents are further off than hype implies.
insights.quote: that is an unbounded security risk that I don't think anyone's going to be able to take anytime soon

insights.claim: Stauch expects every employee to have a personal agent that delegates to other agents, separate from a work agent much like personal and corporate email, creating tension with enterprise governance.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Agent-to-agent governance is an emerging enterprise software opportunity.

insights.claim: CIOs are pulling back from the initial 'token maxing' era, but Stauch expects aggregate AI spend to keep rising dramatically because most companies are early in adoption and still plan to increase budgets.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Short-term enterprise AI spend pullbacks are not a structural demand peak.

insights.claim: Customers' main ask is proof of ROI, and no one has figured out how to measure what tokens buy; Serval prices on workflows run rather than tokens, which reflect verbosity and inefficiency.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Outcome-based pricing may displace token-based pricing in enterprise AI apps.

insights.claim: Companies that tried to build core systems of record in-house with AI coding tools found enterprise software expensive to build and maintain, so build-versus-buy economics still favor buying non-core software.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Core SaaS systems of record are less threatened by in-house AI builds than feared.
insights.quote: it's quite expensive to build and maintain enterprise software

insights.claim: Stauch expects a SaaS apocalypse concentrated in point solutions and middleware, with companies shrinking from hundreds of SaaS apps to a couple dozen, while ERP, HRIS, ITSM and CRM categories survive with a new generation of incumbents.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Small-cap point-solution SaaS is most at risk; category leaders face replacement by AI-native challengers rather than extinction.

insights.claim: Serval productizes features only when it sees many customers building the same automation, such as detecting conflicting knowledge base articles or automatically reclaiming unused software licenses.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: License reclamation automation directly threatens seat-based SaaS revenue.

insights.claim: Serval deploys a deployment strategist and deployed engineer on site and has built an ongoing 'Pro Serval' automation engineering services team because demand for automation work is effectively unlimited.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: AI-native vendors are internalizing implementation work that consultancies traditionally captured.

insights.claim: Serval has no product function; engineers sit in customer Slack channels and most join customer calls daily, decentralizing product decisions to adapt in real time.
insights.speaker: Jake Stauch (Serval)
insights.so_what: Org design is being reshaped around speed of customer feedback in AI markets.
